title: Spain general strike: how 50 years of industrial action shaped Spain’s post-Franco democracy
content:
The end of the Franco dictatorship profoundly changed labour relations in Spain. Under Franco, trade unions were wholly authoritarian, and there was only one permitted union, the Spanish Syndical Organisation or “Sindicato Vertical”. But after Franco’s death in 1975 and the subsequent transition to democracy, trade unions and employers’ organisations received full constitutional recognition as the main players in collective bargaining.

During the transition to democracy, which lasted from 1977 to 1982, employers and unions engaged in social dialogue with the aim of consolidating Spain’s young democracy, and to mitigate the severe economic crisis that began in 1977. The crisis stemmed from overproduction and a sharp rise in oil prices, leading to soaring production costs and high inflation and unemployment.

This social dialogue, known as concertación, ensured social peace, and brought about multiple landmark labour agreements in the early 1980s.

title: How decades of US ‘forever war’ led to the Republicans’ midterm losses
content:
After the 1991 Gulf War, Saddam Hussein, the former president of Iraq, declared “dignified victory” despite a military defeat. He had survived the invasion, while his adversary George HW Bush was facing a recession at home. Bush would go on to lose the 1992 elections to Bill Clinton, who swept to victory with the slogan: “It’s the economy, stupid”.

Even with Iraq’s armed forces devastated, Saddam was able to frame the military defeat as success: not even a coalition of 42 nations could unseat him. Following huge Republican losses in the 2026 US midterm elections, the Islamic Republic of Iran could claim a similar victory, even with the death of its Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei.

In 2024, Donald Trump ran on an electoral promise of “no more wars”. Two years later, American voters dealt his party a resounding defeat. Not only did Trump begin a war with Iran, but that war is fast becoming another “forever war” with no clear end in sight.

title: Artificial intelligence is desperately seeking its narrative
content:
Since the foundational work of Austrian economist Joseph Schumpeter, research has distinguished invention from innovation by its practical implementation. Whether an innovation spreads, however, depends partly on its social acceptance and how its uses are perceived. Without such acceptance, even a promising technology may remain confined to scientific experiments and investors’ speculation. To gain public support, an innovation needs a compelling narrative capable of generating interest, if not enthusiasm. Artificial intelligence illustrates this phenomenon: while its narrative is still taking shape, its social acceptability is increasingly contested.

In July 2026, Le Monde diplomatique declared that “The AI backlash has begun”. The initial sense of wonder generated by ChatGPT has increasingly given way to broader public unease about AI’s social consequences, from its effects on work, education and information to concerns about privacy, the environment and the growing power of technology companies. In this emerging narrative, AI appears as a “digital Moloch” whose costs are borne collectively while its benefits accrue to only a handful of oligarchs.

title: Why young protesters in France are turning against TV channel CNews
content:
On November 5, as secondary school students gathered in Paris for another day of demonstrations, a journalist associated with French media outlet CNews met an unusually hostile reception. Protesters shouted for him to leave, and police officers reportedly asked the journalist to stop heckling the crowd.

What happens when a protest movement turns against the media covering it? In France, students are challenging the government’s education policies and increasingly the news outlets through which their demands reach the public. A petition calling for CNews to be taken off air has gathered more than a million signatures. Petitions and headlines show how much attention the movement commands, but for the protesters themselves, however, the terms of their visibility are part of the problem.

title: Research on migration is going unheard – how can we remedy that?
content:
KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • Policymakers do listen to research, but evidence is only one part of the decision-making process. Public opinion, political pressures, values and competing priorities also shape migration policies.

  • How research is communicated matters. Evidence that is presented neutrally can help to build trust among citizens whose concerns and values must also be weighed in the balance.

title: Europe’s protest wave looks like 1968, but the demands are fundamentally different
content:
Spain’s November 11 general strike, called in response to a housing crisis, stagnant wages and rising living costs, is part of a much wider European story. Student-led protests in countries across the continent have spread from schools and universities into broad alliances with trade unions and housing campaigners.

France has seen large-scale unrest, initially linked to conditions in schools. German pupils have mobilised against conscription, thousands have marched in Greece over public education failures, and Serbia’s student protest movement has reshaped its national politics.

The obvious historical parallel is 1968. Then, as now, European student protests spread beyond campuses, crossed borders and drew workers into mass mobilisation. Politicians warned of social breakdown.

This comparison is not wrong. But focusing only on the similarities risks missing an important distinction between the two moments: that the grievances of the protesters are fundamentally different.

title: Don’t wash your laundry at teatime – why planning energy use can reduce your bills
content:
For decades, judging a home’s energy performance meant asking one question: how much does it use? Labels such as energy performance certificates still ask only that.

But homes are changing. Add solar panels, a battery or an electric car, and a house starts to generate, store and sell electricity. Meanwhile, what that electricity costs depends more and more on the clock. Since June 2026, Ireland’s largest suppliers have had to offer tariffs that change every half hour. In the UK, households pay about 26p for each unit they buy, but solar owners can be paid as little as a few pence for each unit they sell.

The question has shifted from how much energy is being used to when is it being consumed? Every building is now an energy system. The clearest example of what that means is a long way from Europe.

In Pakistan, an estimated 7.3 million households, nearly one in five, now have solar panels. In the year to June 2025, panels on homes, shops, farm sheds and small factories produced the equivalent of 46% of all electricity sold through the national grid. Three lessons stand out.

title: AI could transform mathematics, but humans will still need to be in the loop
content:
OpenAI recently announced that one of its AI models solved one of the hardest problems in modern mathematics: the Navier–Stokes problem. The equations at the heart of this problem describe the movement of fluids like water and, according to the scientific definition, air.

The Navier-Stokes equations are essential to understanding phenomena such as ocean currents, blood circulation, and airflow over airplane wings. Yet, mathematicians have struggled for decades to determine whether coherent solutions to these equations exist.

It was for this reason that the US-based Clay Mathematics Institute, which is dedicated to disseminating mathematical knowledge, chose the Navier-Stokes problem as one of its seven Millennium Prize Problems.

These are the most important and challenging unsolved problems in modern mathematics, with a prize of US$1 million (£746,000; €895,000) offered for the first correct solution to each. A problem that resisted generations of mathematicians thus has apparently been solved by artificial intelligence.

title: Why Europe is building both a digital euro and a new mobile payment network
content:
Sending money from your phone seems simple: just choose a contact, enter an amount, and press confirm. But behind these apparently simple actions lie national payment systems that are not always interoperable.

In Europe, the Madrid-based European Network for Payments (ENP) has been established to link five mobile payment solutions operating in 13 European countries: Bizum (Spain), Bancomat (Italy), SIBS-MB WAY (Portugal), Vipps MobilePay (Norway, Denmark, Sweden and Finland) and EPI/Wero (Germany, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Austria).

The combined infrastructure of these organisations covers more than 70% of the population of the EU and Norway, serving a total of around 130 million active users.

The ENP’s rollout will be gradual, beginning with payment between individuals before progressing to online shopping and brick-and-mortar businesses.

But as the EU gets ready to launch the digital euro over the next few years, the question that will spring to mind for many is: Why bother?

title: What the US midterms result means for the Ukraine war
content:
The US midterm elections have shifted the balance of power in Congress, delivering a massive blow to Donald Trump and his Republican party. This has implications both at home and possibly abroad, including for US policy towards Ukraine; an issue that was hardly mentioned during the campaigns.

But even if Ukraine did not figure much in the election, the question in US politics of what to do about the war has not gone away. Indeed, in the weeks and months before the result was announced, Trump had been busily rowing back on US support for Ukraine. This was despite much opposition, even from some Republicans.

Crucial intelligence to Kyiv about Russian strikes was cut off, before later being reinstated, while critical military aid was reduced. Trump also decided to suspend several sanctions on Russia.

This move was denounced by President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine as only helping Russia, but justified by Trump as being “in the national interests of the United States” and also a decision that might help his party’s electoral chances by reducing gas prices.

title: Why Mark Carney is still betting big on Europe
content:
When European Union officials Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa recently joined Mark Carney on the docks of Montréal’s Old Port for the Canada-EU Summit, Canada’s prime minister presented closer ties with the EU as a good deal for Canadian households.

He argued a closer relationship promised more choices and lower costs for families at a time when American tariffs are causing pain on both sides of the Atlantic.

In April 2025, my colleague, Léandre Benoit, and I argued that the newly elected Carney would pursue a pragmatic and globally engaged liberalism, definitively aligned with Europe. The Montréal summit confirms that alignment.

The meeting’s firmest commitments concern democracy, while much of its economic measures are still to be carried out. With autocracies gaining ground around the world, and with Trump’s United States no longer a reliable ally — although that may shift with the Democratic rout in the U.S. midterm elections — Canada and the EU have found in each other stable liberal partners who take democracy seriously.
